name: The aristocratic rebel
plain_explanation: Unlike a hungry peasant or worker who rebels simply because they want food, land, or basic justice, the 'aristocratic rebel' already has enough to eat; their discontent comes instead from a deeper, more abstract grievance -- a sense that the whole order of the world, or of God's government of it, is intolerable -- which can take the form of grand cosmic self-assertion or (in those with lingering religious belief) outright Satanism.
precise_definition: Russell's category for a type of revolutionary or rebellious figure, distinct from the leader of a hungry, materially deprived (peasant or proletarian) revolt, whose discontent -- possibly rooted in an unconscious love of power -- takes the conscious form of a critique of the government of the world so deep that it produces either Titanic cosmic self-assertion or, in the religiously inclined, Satanism; Byron is presented as its historical exemplar, both traits being found in him.
why_it_mattered: It lets Russell explain why a poet of sometimes 'poor' verse and 'tawdry' sentiment (in Russell's own literary judgment) could nonetheless become a major force shaping nineteenth- and twentieth-century political and philosophical feeling, especially on the Continent, feeding 'a long series of revolutionary movements, from the Carbonari after the fall of Napoleon to Hitler's coup in 1933.'
historical_origin: Developed by Russell as an interpretive category for this chapter, illustrated through Byron's life and verse.
associated_philosopher: Lord Byron (as exemplar); developed philosophically later by Schopenhauer and Nietzsche
examples: Byron's Satanic self-identification with Cain and Manfred
Byron's Corsair, a sage-like pirate-hero who 'hated man too much to feel remorse'
competing_positions: The materially motivated peasant or proletarian rebel (as in Marx), whose 'values remain primitive: the good is enough to eat, and the rest is talk'
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell traces this type forward to Nietzsche, and politically to a lineage running 'from the Carbonari after the fall of Napoleon to Hitler's coup in 1933.'
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly: Russell links the aristocratic-rebel temperament to nationalism and, eventually, fascist politics, and notes its religious form as Satanism.
